posts.title: Re-proofing a Waxed Jacket
posts.excerpt: A practical guide from our Rotterdam workshop on applying paraffin wax to restore weather resistance to an eight-ounce cotton field jacket.
posts.content:
At our workshop at Rijnhaven Works, Unit 4, Kadeweg 18 in Rotterdam, waxed jackets arrive at our counter throughout every autumn. Outdoor workers, landscape crews like the Westpark Grounds Team, and trade joiners rely on these garments to block driving rain and sharp coastal winds. Our waxed field jacket is built from 8 oz waxed cotton with a paraffin finish. When the jacket is brand new, water beads cleanly on the surface and rolls off the shoulders. However, after months of hauling framing timber, pushing through wet brush, and loading work vans, the wax barrier naturally wears thin. Friction across the elbows, creases along the forearms, and heavy contact over the shoulder yoke cause the paraffin coating to dissipate, leaving dry cotton exposed to moisture.

Re-proofing is the straightforward process of restoring that protective paraffin shield into the weave of the cotton cloth. In our Rotterdam workshop, workshop lead Tomasz Wilk oversees every jacket mending and waxing service. We offer complete workshop re-proofing for €32 with a turnaround time of 5 working days, but tradespeople who prefer to maintain their own outerwear can achieve excellent results on a clean workbench. The essential requirement is patience, a solid paraffin wax bar, and an even source of warm air such as a heat gun or domestic hair dryer. Never attempt to wash a waxed jacket in a washing machine or send it to a dry cleaner, because harsh detergents and hot water strip the wax completely and ruin the garment.

Begin by preparing the jacket thoroughly before applying any fresh wax. Use cold tap water, a clean sponge, and a stiff horsehair brush to remove surface soil, dried mud, and sawdust from the cotton duck collar, pocket flaps, and cuff hems. Never use soap or chemical cleaners, as any residue trapped in the fibers prevents new paraffin from bonding with the cotton yarns. Once the garment is clean, allow it to hang naturally on a sturdy timber hanger until the cloth is completely dry. Inspect the seams, metal snaps, and front zipper pull. If any stitching has unraveled, mending those seams before re-proofing ensures the wax seals the repair threads securely.

Work in a warm room on a flat timber table or clean work surface. Warm the wax bar slightly so it slides smoothly across the fabric without crumbling. Rub the wax bar firmly over the cloth in circular strokes, working systematically across one section at a time. Pay close attention to the high-wear areas that take the brunt of rainy shifts: the top of the shoulders, the upper back, the outside seams of the sleeves, and the front pockets. The cloth will show a pale, frosted layer of wax on the surface as you work. This visual guide shows where coverage is thorough and where dry patches remain.

Once a section is covered, use warm air to melt the wax into the cotton weave. Direct the heat evenly across the surface until the white wax turns clear and sinks deeply into the fibers. Keep the heat source moving steadily to avoid scorching the cloth. Work the melted wax into seam lines, pocket edges, and armhole joints with a clean cloth. After the entire jacket has been treated, hang it on a hanger in a warm area away from direct sunlight for a full day to allow the paraffin to cure. The jacket will emerge slightly darker, weather-resistant, and ready for another season of tough shifts.
